deep.reconstruction:
The page is not a derivation. It is pure tabulation, page 4 of a continuous table (previous page: arguments 160–240; next page: 320–400). It lists rectangular equatorial coordinates of the Sun (geocentric X, Y, Z), with the mean distance equal to 10000. The argument runs from 240 to 320 in steps of 1.

What the argument is (my reconstruction, checked numerically against the table):
- The x-coordinate passes through zero at argument ≈188.9 (previous page) and ≈389.6 (next page).
- y passes through zero at ≈291.4 (this page, marked by the horizontal rule after 291).
- At argument 400 the radius vector is sqrt(1649²+8891²+3859²) ≈ 9832 ≈ 1−e, i.e. perigee.
- A full revolution therefore spans 400 units. The argument is the Sun's mean anomaly M in centesimal degrees (grads), with M=0 at perigee.

Model that reproduces the table (my reconstruction):
- True anomaly: v = M + 2e sin M + (5/4)e² sin 2M + …, with e ≈ 0.0168.
- Radius: R = (1−e²)/(1+e cos v).
- Longitude: λ = v + ϖ, with perigee longitude ϖ ≈ 279.6° (the c.1809 value).
- Coordinates:
  - x = R cos λ
  - y = R sin λ cos ε
  - z = R sin λ sin ε
  - obliquity ε ≈ 23°28′
- All values are ×10⁴. Column headers give the signs, since only magnitudes are written.
- On the left half (240–280) x<0, y>0, z>0, so λ runs from about 134° to 168°.
- On the right half (280–320) x<0 throughout. y and z change sign at λ = 180° (autumnal equinox), between arguments 291 and 292; hence the ± headings and the ruled line.

Numerical checks against the table:
- At M = 300 grads = 270°: v ≈ 268.09°, λ ≈ 187.7°, R ≈ 1.0003. This gives x ≈ −9912, y ≈ −1234, z ≈ −536. Table: 9912, 1235, 536.
- At 290 the radius vector is sqrt(10027²+199²+86²) ≈ 10029, and |x| reaches its maximum 10027 there. This is consistent with λ ≈ 178.8°.
- The ratio z/y equals tan ε ≈ 0.4341 throughout (e.g. 2877/6627, 1725/3975, 1204/2775).
- First and second differences in all six columns are smooth, as expected for a table computed directly or by systematic subtabulation.

Purpose: a standing table of solar coordinates for reducing observations. It is apparently arranged by mean anomaly so that it serves any year once the mean anomaly is known. Such X, Y, Z of the Sun are exactly what Gauss's orbit-determination methods (Theoria Motus, 1809) require: geocentric places of planets and comets combined with heliocentric orbits. The step in grads (0.9°, about 0.913 days) is a convenient decimal division.
errors: Argument 312, x column: table has 9450. Interpolating from 9504 (311) and 9399 (313) with the prevailing second difference (≈ −2.5) gives ≈9453, and direct computation also gives ≈9453. Either it is a slip of about 3 units or the last digit is a 3 misread as 0. Differences around it read −49, −54, −51, −56, which flags the irregularity.
Otherwise no errors found. All other columns have smooth differences, and z/y = tan 23°28′ to within rounding everywhere checked.

results.what: Table of geocentric rectangular equatorial coordinates of the Sun (X, Y, Z, radius unit 10000), argument = mean anomaly in centesimal degrees, e≈0.0168, perigee longitude ≈279.6°, obliquity ≈23°28′
results.modern_name: Solar rectangular coordinates table (Sun's equatorial X, Y, Z from the elliptic solar theory / equation of centre)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard astronomical practice; such tables appear in ephemerides (e.g. Berliner Astronomisches Jahrbuch) from the early 19th century; Gauss's Theoria Motus (1809) systematically uses the Sun's X, Y, Z

results.what: Use of a 400-part (centesimal) division of the mean anomaly as table argument
results.usually_credited_to: French decimal reform (Borda, Delambre, Laplace era, 1790s)

deep.surprise_reason: A routine computational table of the Sun's equatorial coordinates of the kind Gauss needed for orbit work in 1809. The only mildly notable feature is the centesimal mean-anomaly argument; there is no new mathematics.
